questions.stem:
The discrete random variable $X$ can only take the values 1, 2, 3 and 4
For these values the cumulative distribution function is defined by

$\mathrm{F}(x) = kx^2$ for $x = 1, 2, 3, 4$

where $k$ is a constant.

parts.label: a
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) M1: writing or using $\mathrm{F}(4)=1$
A1: $\frac{1}{16}$ or 0.0625 (Answer only scores 2 out of 2)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- $\mathrm{F}(4)=1$ M1; $4^2k=1\Rightarrow k=\frac{1}{16}$ A1

parts.label: b
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: correct use of $\mathrm{F}(x)$ to find $\mathrm{P}(X=2, 3, \text{ or } 4)$ (can follow through their $k$, $3k$, $5k$, $7k$). May be implied by at least two correct probabilities or correct follow through.
A1: for a fully correct probability distribution. Allow exact decimals. Ignore incorrect or missing labels if table is all correct.
$\mathrm{P}(X=1)=\frac{1}{16}$ (0.0625), $\mathrm{P}(X=2)=\frac{3}{16}$ (0.1875), $\mathrm{P}(X=3)=\frac{5}{16}$ (0.3125), $\mathrm{P}(X=4)=\frac{7}{16}$ (0.4375)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- e.g. $\mathrm{P}(X=2)=\mathrm{F}(2)-\mathrm{F}(1)=\frac{4}{16}-\frac{1}{16}=\frac{3}{16}$ M1

questions.stem:
A company employs 90 administrators. The length of time that they have been employed by the company and their gender are summarised in the table below.

$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Length of time employed, } x \text{ years} & \text{Female} & \text{Male}\\ \hline x<4 & 9 & 16\\ \hline 4 \leqslant x<10 & 14 & 20\\ \hline 10 \leqslant x & 7 & 24\\ \hline\end{array}$

One of the 90 administrators is selected at random.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the probability that the administrator is female.
(1)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Given that the administrator has been employed by the company for less than 4 years, find the probability that this administrator is male.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: for a correct ratio expression with at least one correct probability substituted or for a correct ratio of probabilities. num>denom is M0
A1: $\frac{16}{25}$ or 0.64 (Correct answer scores 2 out of 2)
$\mathrm{P}(\text{Male}\mid<4\text{ years})=\frac{\mathrm{P}(\text{Male}\cap<4\text{ years})}{\mathrm{P}(<4\text{ years})}=\frac{16/(90)}{(16+9)/(90)}=\frac{16}{25}$ oe

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Given that the administrator has been employed by the company for less than 10 years, find the probability that this administrator is male.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) M1: for a correct ratio expression with at least one correct probability substituted or for a correct ratio of probabilities. num>denom is M0.
A1: $\frac{36}{59}$ or condone awrt 0.610 (must be 3sf) (Correct answer gets 2 out of 2)
$\mathrm{P}(\text{Male}\mid<10\text{ years})=\frac{\mathrm{P}(\text{Male}\cap<10\text{ years})}{\mathrm{P}(<10\text{ years})}=\frac{(20+16)/(90)}{(9+16+14+20)/(90)}=\frac{36}{59}$

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) State, with a reason, whether or not the event 'selecting a male' is independent of the event 'selecting an administrator who has been employed by the company for less than 4 years'.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) 1st M1: for stating all of the required numerical probabilities for a correct test which must be labelled. The probabilities must be correct or correct ft from (b)
(If attempting the first test, $\mathrm{P}(\text{Male}\mid<4\text{ years})='\frac{16}{25}'$ was found in part (b) and need not be fully restated here).
$\mathrm{P}(\text{Male}\mid<4\text{ years})='\frac{16}{25}'$, $\mathrm{P}(\text{Male})=\frac{60}{90}$ or $\mathrm{P}(<4\text{ years}\mid\text{Male})=\frac{16}{60}$, $\mathrm{P}(<4\text{ years})=\frac{25}{90}$ or $\mathrm{P}(\text{Male}\cap<4\text{ years})=\frac{16}{90}$, $\mathrm{P}(\text{Male})=\frac{60}{90}$, $\mathrm{P}(<4\text{ years})=\frac{25}{90}$
2nd M1: for use of a correct test. Must see the product if attempting the 3rd test.
A1: for correct test with all probabilities correct and a correct conclusion.
$\mathrm{P}(\text{M}\mid<4)\neq \mathrm{P}(\text{M})$ or $\mathrm{P}(<4\mid \text{M})\neq \mathrm{P}(<4)$ or $\mathrm{P}(\text{Male}\cap<4\text{ years})\neq \mathrm{P}(\text{M})\times \mathrm{P}(<4)$ so not independent.
NB Use of A and B throughout scores M0M0A0 unless A and B are explicitly defined.

questions.stem:
A bag contains 19 red beads and 1 blue bead only.

Linda selects a bead at random from the bag. She notes its colour and replaces the bead in the bag. She then selects a second bead at random from the bag and notes its colour.

Find the probability that

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) exactly one bead selected is red.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: for a correct equivalent expression $\frac{1}{20}\times \frac{19}{20}+\frac{19}{20}\times \frac{1}{20}$
A1: $\frac{19}{200}$ or 0.095
$\mathrm{P}(\text{exactly 1 red})=2\times \frac{1}{20}\times \frac{19}{20}=\frac{19}{200}$ oe

parts.label: c
parts.text:
In another bag there are 9 beads, 4 of which are green and the rest are yellow.

Linda selects 3 beads from this bag at random without replacement.

(c) Find the probability that 2 of these beads are yellow and 1 is green.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) B1: for $3\times \ldots$ or for the sum of exactly 3 identical products attempted
M1: for any one product correct
A1: $\frac{10}{21}$ (allow awrt 0.476 from correct working)
$\mathrm{P}(\text{2 yellow and 1 green})=3\times \frac{4}{9}\times \frac{5}{8}\times \frac{4}{7}=\frac{10}{21}$ oe

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Linda replaces the 3 beads and then selects another 4 at random without replacement.

(d) Find the probability that at least 1 of the beads is green.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) 1st M1: $\frac{5}{9}\times \frac{4}{8}\times \frac{3}{7}\times \frac{2}{6}$
2nd M1: Use of $1-p$ (where $p$ is a product of 4 probabilities)
A1: $\frac{121}{126}$ (condone awrt 0.960 must be at least 3sf from correct working)
$\mathrm{P}(\text{All beads are yellow})=\frac{5}{9}\times \frac{4}{8}\times \frac{3}{7}\times \frac{2}{6}$
$\mathrm{P}(\text{At least 1 bead is green})=1-\mathrm{P}(\text{All beads are yellow})=1-\frac{5}{9}\times \frac{4}{8}\times \frac{3}{7}\times \frac{2}{6}=\frac{121}{126}$
OR 1st M1: List all 15 favourable outcomes and at least one correct product (YYYG)$\times$4 [(YYGY), (YGYY), (GYYY)]; (YYGG)$\times$6 [(YGYG), (YGGY), (GYYG), (GYGY), (GGYY)]; (GGYG)$\times$4 [(GGGY), (YGGG), (GYGG)]; (GGGG)
2nd M1: Sum all 15 correct probabilities
A1: $\frac{121}{126}$ (condone awrt 0.960 must be at least 3sf from correct working)

questions.stem:
Police measure the speed of cars passing a particular point on a motorway.
The random variable $X$ is the speed of a car.

$X$ is modelled by a normal distribution with mean 55 mph (miles per hour).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Draw a sketch to illustrate the distribution of $X$. Label the mean on your sketch.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) 1st B1: for a reasonable sketch of a symmetric, bell shaped curve which does not cross the $x$-axis (ignore any vertical axis drawn)
2nd B1 (dependent): dependent on previous B1 for 55 labelled at the centre of the $x$-axis

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The speed limit on the motorway is 70 mph. Car drivers can choose to travel faster than the speed limit but risk being caught by the police.

The distribution of $X$ has a standard deviation of 20 mph.

(b) Find the percentage of cars that are travelling faster than the speed limit.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: for standardising with 70, 55, 20 (allow +/−)
M1: use of $1-p$ (must be a probability so $1-0.67$ is M0)
A1: awrt 0.227 or 22.7%
$\mathrm{P}(X>70)=\mathrm{P}\left(Z>\frac{70-55}{20}\right)=\mathrm{P}(Z>0.75)=1-0.7734=0.2266$

parts.label: c
parts.text:
The fastest 1% of car drivers will be banned from driving.

(c) Show that the lowest speed, correct to 3 significant figures, for a car driver to be banned is 102 mph. Show your working clearly.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) M1: for standardising with 55, 20 and equating to $z$-value $|z|>2$
B1: for 2.3263 (or better) used and compatible sign with their standardisation.
A1: for awrt 102 which must come from a $z$-value in the range $2.32 \leqslant z \leqslant 2.34$
$\mathrm{P}(X>b)=0.01$
$\frac{b-55}{20}=2.3263$
$b=101.526$ **Given answer 102**

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Car drivers will just be given a caution if they are travelling at a speed $m$ such that

$\mathrm{P}(70<X<m)=0.1315$

(d) Find the value of $m$. Show your working clearly.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) 1st M1: for a correct expression for $\mathrm{P}(X<m)$ (e.g. $0.1315+'0.7734'$) or $\mathrm{P}(X>m)=0.0951$ or sight of 0.9049 (may be implied by sight of 1.31)
2nd M1: for standardising with 55, 20 and equating to a $z$-value $|z|>1$
B1: 1.31 (1.31018… from calc) used and compatible sign with their standardisation.
A1: awrt 81.2
$\mathrm{P}(70<X<m)=0.1315$
$\mathrm{P}(X<m)-\mathrm{P}(X<70)=0.1315$
$\mathrm{P}\left(Z<\frac{m-55}{20}\right)=0.9049$
$\frac{m-55}{20}=1.31$
$m=81.2$
